title: Living in the forests
hookLine: with a price on their heads, Sikhs lived on horseback in forests and deserts

cards: A saddle for a pillow. A blanket that is also a cloak. A cooking pot tied behind, and the reins never far from your hand, even asleep.
Tradition says that in these years whole Sikh families had no address at all. The governors in Lahore had put a price on a Sikh's head, and a village that sheltered them could be punished.
So the Khalsa moved into the places nobody wanted to follow: thick forests along the rivers, the dry country to the south, the edges of the desert.

teach.b: What did that life look like? Tradition remembers bands of horsemen, called jathas, moving from one hiding place to the next, never staying long.
They ate what they could find, or what friendly villagers slipped them in the dark. They slept in shifts. When soldiers came close, they scattered and met again somewhere agreed in advance.
A horse was not a possession. It was the house, the escape, the way to bring food home. And here's the surprising part: out of that hard life came humor.

teach.h: KHALSA BOLE: A JOKE AGAINST HARDSHIP.
teach.b: The Khalsa developed its own way of speaking, sometimes called Khalsa bole, the Khalsa's words, and some of it is a joke against hardship. Some tellings say a handful of dry chickpeas was called almonds.
A lone rider might call himself an army. It sounds like bravado, and maybe it was.
But it was also a way of refusing to let the hunt decide how they felt: the chardi kala this path met in the hills after Lohgarh, turned into a joke. The Gurus' hymns were with them too.
Riders who knew them by heart could recite the morning and evening prayers in a forest clearing as easily as in a town.

The Name, the tradition says, does not. Where the riders stopped, the sangat was. Some readers hear one more thing in these stories: a reminder that a roof, a bed and a door that locks are not ordinary at all.

how: Sikhs tell stories of the forest years in gurdwaras and at home, and remember them in the daily Ardas, which honors those who held to the faith through persecution.

o: rising spirits that a hard life can't sink
a band of horsemen always on the move
the Khalsa's coded speech and jokes

games.q: life on the move — tap the pairs.

riders recited the hymns by heart in forest clearings.
the Khalsa joked about its hardships
Khalsa bole, the Khalsa's words, turned hunger and danger into humor.
villages that sheltered Sikhs were safe from punishment

games.q: you're a rider in a jatha. soldiers are closing in on your camp. what do you do?
o: stand and defend the camp to the end.
scatter and meet again at a place agreed in advance.
games.why: tradition says the jathas scattered and regrouped. a horse made it possible: it was the house and the escape.

practice: Notice what is above you, a ceiling, a roof, and the walls and door around you, and feel the floor holding you up, dry and level.

Let your attention move slowly through the room, the light, the warmth or the cool, a place to sleep tonight, letting each one register as a gift. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for each thing you notice.

wordCard.voice: Chardi kala, rising spirits. The years when the hunted Khalsa had no fixed home, living on horseback in forests and deserts, with the Name and a joke for company.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: chardi kala, rising spirits, staying high in hard times.

carryVoice: Your line: home was a horse. Dry chickpeas, called almonds. Eight hundred forty-nine days, and counting.
